content: The Keck Graduate Institute of Applied Life Sciences (KGI) is a specialized graduate school located in Claremont, California. It was established in 1997 with an initial startup grant of $50 million provided by the W. M. Keck Foundation. KGI is part of the Claremont Colleges consortium. The institution offers a Professional Science Master’s degree known as the Master of Bioscience (MBS) and a PhD in Applied Life Sciences. The MBS program spans two years and combines scientific, engineering, and business curricula, culminating in a Team Master’s Project (TMP) that is sponsored by one of KGI’s industry partners. The Team Master’s Project serves as the capstone of the MBS program. In this project, teams of three to five students collaborate with sponsoring companies to address real-world challenges. These projects typically encompass both business and technical components. For instance, students may be tasked with validating a new technology and devising a strategy for its market penetration. The specific deliverables for each TMP are negotiated between the student team and the company liaison. Graduates of the KGI MBS program have been employed by prominent companies such as Amgen, Genentech, Beckman Coulter, and Eli Lilly. Their career paths often include roles in marketing, regulatory affairs, business development, project management, or research. KGI is accredited by the Accrediting Commission for Senior Colleges and Universities of the Western Association of Schools and Colleges. Notable members of KGI’s advisory council include Bruce Alberts, Simon Ramo, John Hopfield, Alfred Mann, and J. Craig Venter. Arthur Riggs, one of the founding scientists of Genentech, serves as a trustee of the institute. Ionian Technologies, founded in 2000, was the first spin-off company to commercialize technology developed at KGI. Ionian specializes in molecular diagnostics for emerging and infectious diseases. In 2004, the company was awarded a contract to develop a handheld biothreat detector using isothermal DNA amplification. Other startups originating from KGI include Zuyder Pharmaceuticals and Claremont BioSciences. KGI students Peter Vandeventer and Christopher Warner were recipients of the prestigious Science, Mathematics, and Research for Transformation (SMART) scholarships from the U.S. Department of Defense to support their PhD research in biodefense. Out of 1,600 applicants nationwide, only 100 SMART scholarships were awarded. In June 2006, KGI received a $100,000 grant from the Michael J. Connell Foundation of Pasadena to support Professor Animesh Ray’s project titled “Creating a Comprehensive Integrated Database for Multidisciplinary Data on the Avian Influenza.” In April 2005, the Amgen Foundation donated $2 million to establish a teaching and research-scale bioprocessing center at KGI. The W. M. Keck Foundation endowed a professorship in honor of George B. Rathmann to direct the center. Dr. Matthew S. Croughan was appointed as the center’s first director in January 2006. Additionally, KGI received an $8.8 million grant through the National Science Foundation’s Frontiers in Integrative Biological Research (FIBR) program to study the basis of modularity in biology. The decision to establish KGI as the seventh Claremont College faced some opposition initially. Faculty members from other Claremont Colleges objected to its lack of tenure, while environmentalists opposed its plans to build on the Bernard Field Station, an area of undeveloped scrubland. The environmental concerns were largely resolved when KGI agreed not to develop a significant portion of the land for at least 50 years. Over time, other opposition gradually diminished.
